title: Atanasoff-Berry Computer and Colossus
text:
CHAPTER 4. VACUUM TUBES AND THE FIRST ELECTRONIC COMPUTERS
SECTION 4.2. ATANASOFF-BERRY COMPUTER AND COLOSSUS

Who built the first electronic computer? The honest answer is "it depends on what you count," and two machines of the early 1940s show why. The Atanasoff-Berry Computer in Iowa was electronic and binary but not programmable. Colossus in Britain was electronic and programmable in a limited way but built for one job, codebreaking. Both used vacuum tubes in the switching modes described in Section 4.1, both were largely unknown to the public for decades, and both force us to be precise about definitions.

PART A. THE ATANASOFF-BERRY COMPUTER

1. The problem: linear equations

John Vincent Atanasoff (1903-1995) was a professor of mathematics and physics at Iowa State College in Ames. His students' research in physics needed solutions of systems of simultaneous linear equations, for which hand methods with desk calculators were painfully slow. A system of n equations in n unknowns,

    a11 x1 + a12 x2 + ... + a1n xn = b1
    ...
    an1 x1 + an2 x2 + ... + ann xn = bn

is solved by Gaussian elimination: use one equation to eliminate a variable from all the others, repeat, then back-substitute. The work grows roughly as n^3 operations, so a system of 29 equations, the size Atanasoff targeted, needs on the order of ten thousand multiply-add operations, each of them error-prone by hand.

(It is worth pausing on this. Solving linear systems and multiplying matrices is exactly the computational core of modern machine learning too. The first electronic digital calculator was built for linear algebra, and so, in a sense, are today's AI accelerators.)

2. Design ideas

Atanasoff later described how, during the winter of 1937-38, after a long nighttime drive that ended at a roadhouse across the state line in Illinois, he settled several key principles. Whatever the exact circumstances, the design he arrived at had these features:

  - Electronic computation using vacuum tubes, for speed.
  - Binary arithmetic, rather than decimal, for simplicity of the electronic circuits.
  - Memory separate from computation.
  - Regenerative capacitor memory: bits stored as charges on capacitors, periodically refreshed.
  - Logical (rather than counting) operations for arithmetic, that is, adders built from switching logic.

He began building a prototype in 1939 with a graduate student in electrical engineering, Clifford Berry (1918-1963). An 11-tube prototype was demonstrated in October 1939, and the full machine was built in the basement of the physics building between 1939 and 1942, funded by Iowa State and a $5,000 grant from the Research Corporation of New York.

3. How the ABC worked

Memory. Two drums rotated on a common shaft once per second. Each drum carried 1,600 capacitors arranged in 32 bands of 50 (30 active bands plus 2 spares). One band held one 50-bit binary number, so each drum held 30 numbers, and the two drums held the coefficients of two equations being combined. A capacitor charged one way represented 1, the other way 0.

Capacitors leak, so stored charge decays. Atanasoff's solution was to read and rewrite every bit once per revolution: "jogging" the memory, as he called it. This is the principle of refresh, exactly how the dynamic RAM (DRAM) in your laptop works today: each DRAM bit is a tiny capacitor that must be refreshed every few tens of milliseconds. The ABC is often credited as the first use of regenerative capacitor memory.

Arithmetic. As the drums turned, the 30 numbers of a band position passed under brushes in parallel, and 30 add-subtract units, built from vacuum tubes, operated on corresponding bits at the same time. In effect the ABC had 30 parallel serial adders, processing one bit position of 30 numbers per step. Because the drum turned once per second, the machine performed about 30 additions or subtractions per second, all in parallel. This was a SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) design in modern terminology: the same operation on many data elements at once, like a GPU lane.

Each adder was a full adder (Section 2.2) implemented with tube logic, combining the two bits and the carry, with the carry stored for the next bit position as the drum rotated. Machine numbers were 50-bit fixed-point binary.

Size and parts. The ABC was about the size of a desk and contained, by commonly cited figures, about 280 dual-triode vacuum tubes, 31 thyratrons and about a mile of wire.

Input/output and intermediate storage. Coefficients were entered in decimal on standard IBM 80-column punched cards and converted to binary. Gaussian elimination needs intermediate results stored outside the drums, and for this Atanasoff designed a binary card writer/reader that recorded bits by burning small marks into paper cards with electric sparks. This component never became fully reliable, with an error rate reported as small but too high for large systems.

4. What happened

In 1942 Atanasoff left Iowa State for wartime work at the Naval Ordnance Laboratory in Washington, and work on the ABC stopped before the card system was perfected. The machine was later dismantled. A working replica was built at Iowa State University in the 1990s.

The ABC was not programmable: its sequence of operations was fixed by its design to perform elimination on pairs of equations, with an operator guiding the overall process. It was therefore a special-purpose electronic calculator, not a general-purpose computer.

5. Mauchly, the patent case, and credit

In June 1941 John Mauchly, who would later co-design ENIAC (Section 4.3), visited Atanasoff in Ames for several days, saw the ABC and read its documentation. Years later this visit became central to a major patent lawsuit. Sperry Rand held the ENIAC patent (filed 1947, issued 1964). In Honeywell, Inc. v. Sperry Rand Corp., a US federal district court ruled on October 19, 1973, that the ENIAC patent was invalid, on several grounds, including that Eckert and Mauchly had derived the subject matter of the electronic digital computer from Atanasoff.

Historians continue to debate how much ENIAC actually owed to the ABC. ENIAC's design (decimal ring counters, plugboard programming, a very different architecture) is quite unlike the ABC's. What is clear is that the court decision put the invention of the electronic digital computer in the public domain and restored Atanasoff's reputation. The lesson for engineers: document your work and its dates, because priority disputes happen and they matter.

PART B. COLOSSUS

6. Why Colossus was needed

Section 3.3 described the Lorenz teleprinter cipher ("Tunny") and how Bill Tutte deduced its structure in 1942. To read a Tunny message, codebreakers needed the starting positions of its twelve wheels for that message. W. T. Tutte devised a statistical method to find the settings of the five "chi" wheels first: try each combination of starting positions, compute a particular XOR-based count over the ciphertext, and look for the setting whose count deviated most from what random data would give. The true setting reveals a slight statistical bias that comes from the structure of German plaintext and the irregular motion of the psi wheels.

The counting is simple per character but the volume is huge: thousands of characters of ciphertext for each of many hundreds or thousands of trial settings. Heath Robinson, the first machine built for this at Bletchley Park, read the ciphertext and a key-pattern tape simultaneously with photoelectric readers, but keeping two tapes synchronized at high speed was unreliable.

7. Tommy Flowers's design

Thomas (Tommy) Flowers (1905-1998) was an engineer at the Post Office Research Station at Dollis Hill in London, where he had used vacuum tubes in experimental telephone exchange equipment before the war. His proposal: generate the wheel patterns electronically inside the machine, using tube circuits, so that only the ciphertext tape had to be read, and its own sprocket holes could supply the timing. The machine's clock was derived from the tape.

Many at Bletchley doubted that a machine with well over a thousand valves could run reliably. Flowers's experience told him that valves left switched on and run gently were reliable (Section 4.1). The Post Office built the first Colossus largely on its own resources at Dollis Hill. It contained about 1,600 valves; Max Newman recorded in a memo dated 18 January 1944 that "Colossus arrives today," and it successfully attacked its first message on 5 February 1944.

8. How Colossus worked

  Input. The ciphertext was punched on a loop of paper tape, read photoelectrically at 5,000 characters per second while the tape loop ran continuously.

  Wheel patterns. Thyratron rings and valve circuits generated the patterns of the chi wheels (and later others), which could be set by plug panels and switches.

  Logic. Plugboards and switches selected Boolean functions to be computed between ciphertext bits and wheel-pattern bits: XOR (addition modulo 2), AND, OR and NOT combinations. For each character, the function result was 0 or 1.

  Counting. Electronic counters, built from valve flip-flops in decimal stages, counted how many times the function was 1 during a full pass of the tape. At the end of a pass, if a count exceeded a threshold set by the operator, it was printed on an electric typewriter.

  Stepping through settings. After each pass the machine automatically advanced the trial wheel settings and repeated, so it scanned through all combinations of the chosen wheels' positions.

A simple version of the computation, in plain notation. Let Z(i) be the ciphertext bits of impulse 1 and 2 at character i and chi1(i), chi2(i) the trial chi wheel bits. The machine might count:

    count = number of i such that (Z1(i) XOR Z2(i) XOR chi1(i) XOR chi2(i)) = 0

For random settings, about half the characters give 0. For the correct settings, the count is slightly above half, because of biases in the de-chi'd stream. Detecting that small excess over thousands of characters is a statistical hypothesis test, done electronically.

Mark 2. An improved Colossus Mark 2, with about 2,400 valves, first ran on 1 June 1944, just before D-Day. It processed five copies of the tape stream in parallel using shift registers, which made it about five times faster, effectively 25,000 characters per second. It also included more flexible logic and the ability to make some decisions automatically. By the end of the war ten Colossi were in use at Bletchley Park, and an eleventh was being commissioned.

9. Was Colossus a computer?

Colossus was:

  - electronic (valves throughout its logic and counting);
  - digital and binary in its logic;
  - programmable, in the sense that its Boolean functions, counting conditions and stepping were configured by plugboards and switches rather than built in;
  - built for one family of problems: statistical analysis of Tunny ciphertext.

It did not store programs in memory, it did not do general arithmetic in the way a computer of the late 1940s did, and it is generally not regarded as Turing complete. Its usual modern description is "the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer," with emphasis that it was special-purpose and not a stored-program machine.

10. Secrecy and rediscovery

After the war most Colossi were dismantled on orders to preserve secrecy, and documents were destroyed. Two machines are reported to have gone to GCHQ, the postwar successor to Bletchley, where they remained in use into the 1950s or 1960s. Flowers could not talk about his work and received little recognition for decades; the existence of Colossus was revealed in the 1970s, and many technical details became public only with declassification of documents in 2000, including the "General Report on Tunny" written in 1945 by Jack Good, Donald Michie and Geoffrey Timms. Between 1993 and 2008 a team of volunteers led by Tony Sale rebuilt a working Colossus Mark 2, now regularly demonstrated at The National Museum of Computing at Bletchley Park.

11. Comparing the ABC and Colossus

    Feature              ABC (Iowa, 1939-1942)         Colossus (Britain, 1944)
    -------              ---------------------         ------------------------
    Purpose              linear equations              cipher statistics
    Number system        binary fixed point, 50-bit    binary bits, decimal counters
    Tubes                about 280 + 31 thyratrons     about 1,600 (Mk 1), 2,400 (Mk 2)
    Memory               capacitor drums, refreshed    paper tape loop; valve registers
    Parallelism          30 adders in parallel         5-way parallel stream (Mk 2)
    Programmable         no                            yes, by plugboards and switches
    Stored program       no                            no
    Status after war     dismantled, unknown           dismantled, secret

Both machines show the same engineering pattern seen in modern AI hardware: when a single kind of computation dominates a workload (multiply-accumulate in linear algebra, or bitwise counting in cryptanalysis), a special-purpose parallel electronic machine beats general-purpose ones by large factors.

12. Summary

  - The Atanasoff-Berry Computer (conceived 1937, built 1939-1942 by Atanasoff and Berry) was electronic, binary, used 30 parallel adders and refreshed capacitor-drum memory (an ancestor of DRAM), and solved linear equations; it was not programmable.
  - Mauchly visited Atanasoff in June 1941; in 1973 a US court invalidated the ENIAC patent partly on that basis. Historians debate the actual technical influence.
  - Colossus, designed by Tommy Flowers at Dollis Hill, first ran at Bletchley Park in early 1944 (attacking its first message on 5 February 1944), read tape at 5,000 characters per second, and counted Boolean functions of ciphertext and wheel patterns to find Lorenz settings.
  - Colossus Mark 2 (2,400 valves) ran from 1 June 1944; ten were in use by war's end.
  - Colossus was programmable, electronic and digital but special-purpose and not stored-program; secrecy hid it until the 1970s.
